1:
Nobody thinks the image was solid metal. Gill makes it a shell of plate or a gilded wooden core, since the bulk would otherwise swallow a prodigious quantity of gold; Ellicott supposes wood under thin plates, and observes that the height is out of proportion to the width, so the sixty cubits probably take in the pedestal, as Clarke suspects. Henry turns it round: rich as the king was, he likely could not have afforded solid gold, yet the worshippers of false gods never count the cost of an image, lavishing gold out of the bag in a way that shames our stinginess toward the true God.

Whom it honoured is not recoverable, and three say so. Gill lists the candidates — the king himself, his father, the chief god, or some new deity — and offers motives instead: vanity, a wish to display the monarchy as an image all of gold rather than a head of gold, and a design to contradict the dream that promised his empire an end. Wesley suggests he was clearing himself of the suspicion that he had gone over to the Jews after praising their God. Calvin dismisses as frivolous the guess that the statue was a charm to avert the dream, doubts the king deified himself, and thinks he consecrated it to an existing god; what he is sure of is the mixture of motives, since men who spend on temples say it is for God's honour and are advancing their own.

Henry stands back further. The city was already full of idols and one more was still wanted, which he takes for the standing condition of idolatry: those who leave the one living God find what they set up so unsatisfying that they multiply gods without measure.

The roll of officers divides them by temperament. Keil and Delitzsch work through seven classes with Persian etymologies, making the first the king's chief representatives and the second probably military commanders. Clarke reproduces another scholar's derivations at length, so that one title becomes privy counsellors with free access to the presence and another a body of nobles he compares to the House of Lords. Calvin refuses the exercise: he does not know the derivations, these are plainly names of magistracies, the words are not Hebrew and the Jews know no more of their origin than he does, and the subtler explanations assert nothing but what is frivolous. He says the same of the instruments, that he does not know what kind they were, where Clarke identifies each and quotes a traveller's description of one as a triangle strung with twenty catguts.

The proclamation is read for its reach and threat. Gill thinks one herald could not have carried across such a crowd, so the singular stands for many voices about the plain in different tongues, as Wesley also says. Ellicott takes the three terms for all nations under the empire. Clarke notices something else, that this is the first place in the older Scriptures where time is divided into hours; the Greeks credited the invention to one of their own, who probably had it from the Chaldeans. On the penalty Ellicott notes that burning was not unusual there, and that at a national festival refusal counted as treason.

Calvin sees what the edict did not require: no profession of belief was demanded, and bending the knee was enough. That is why the excuse fails for anyone who bows while privately dissenting, since God asks first for the worship of the mind and then the profession that matches it, and an outward act given to an idol has already alienated a man from true worship. He adds what makes the crowd's compliance intelligible: had the king ordered every temple thrown down and the God of Israel worshipped instead, there would have been tumults everywhere; but at the signal they fell down without a murmur.
8:
Two absences shape the passage, and the commentators worry at both. Henry finds it strange that the three attended at all, knowing what the assembly was for, and answers that they meant to obey as far as obedience could go and to bear their testimony where it would be seen: it was not enough, holding office as they did, merely to refrain from bowing. Daniel's absence he explains loosely, by business or by leave, or by a standing so high that nobody dared complain of him. Clarke agrees that he was probably too eminent to be touched, notes that the other Jews present went unremarked as well, and is certain he was not among the worshippers. Gill places the approach either at the palace or, more likely, out on the plain itself, with the assembly still standing.

Ellicott turns the same absence into an argument about the book. Daniel's conduct in a later chapter puts it beyond question that he would not have joined the rite; perhaps his office as chief of the wise men excused his attendance, perhaps other duties took him away. What Ellicott insists on is what follows from the silence: the book is not written to glorify Daniel, and an author inventing the story would certainly have arranged a miracle to rescue him along with the other three.

Who the accusers were, and why they moved, is where the readings differ in weight. Ellicott distinguishes them from the astrologers, making them native subjects set against the Jewish colonists, and supposes the promotion of three foreigners had been watched with jealousy for some time. Henry offers two guesses, that they were of the class Daniel had eclipsed and so returned evil for the good his prayers had once done them — for their love being their adversaries — or that they simply wanted the offices themselves, since nobody can stand before envy. He adds that we should not find such ingratitude strange, men having dug pits before now for those who interceded to save them. Calvin goes furthest and reads the whole ceremony as a trap. Kings who despise God still arm themselves with religion to hold their subjects, and this statue was set in a public place as a test of whether the Jews would conform. The counsellors were behind it, galled that men who were slaves by right of war had been made prefects over them, and the proof is in the speed of the accusation: nobody discovers so quickly that a particular man has not bowed unless he was standing there to watch him. On that reading the image was raised at their advice, and the snare was laid before the summons went out.

Calvin also sees why only three are named. The charge was probably confined to them because they were the hard case; break these and the rest of the exiles would follow, few among the people being of a temper to stand. The manner of the charge is read for its craft. Henry notes the respectful preface and the loyal compliment, as though the accusers cared for nothing but the king's honour, when what they were urging on him would have ruined him; they take care first to remind him of his own recent law. Gill hears contempt in the bare phrase certain Jews, which sets them down as foreigners, exiles and captives, unfit for trust and never worth the king's notice, with the implication that in promoting them he had blundered. Ellicott reads the mention of their office as doing double work, explaining the king's fury at what looked like ingratitude and exposing the malice of the men who framed the complaint.
13:
The tone of the reply is noticed before its content. Gill hears it as mild and unaffronting, neither insulting the king's gods nor descending to servile fear or flattery. Calvin marks what it cost: with that death set immediately before them they did not swerve, valuing God's glory above their lives, and above a hundred lives had they possessed them. Two of the commentators point to a small formal detail, that the men address the king by his own name. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take it as answering his address to them, and Ellicott adds what it signals — that in a collision between duty to God and a royal edict the distance between king and subject simply closes.

The opening phrase is corrected by nearly everyone. Ellicott gives it as we have no need, meaning that a reply is unnecessary; Clarke expands it into we need not put thee to further trouble, our minds are made up and our answer is ready, and calls this as honest as it was decisive; Wesley makes it plainer still, that debating is useless since the king is resolved to have his will and they are resolved otherwise; Calvin sums it as a declaration that the matter is settled.

The conditional that follows is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and the voices divide over what it claims. Ellicott would drop the word so and read it as one clause: if our God is able to deliver us, he will do so, and if he does not, we still will not serve your gods. On his reading the three are content to leave the outcome with providence and there is not the slightest ground for supposing they expected a miracle; the language implies faithful obedience and nothing more, since they never questioned the power and simply did not know the will. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same place by the grammar, taking the word for able in an ethical sense, the power as bounded by God's own holiness rather than bare omnipotence, which they say the three would never have called into question before a heathen king; and they deny expressly that the answer shows audacity, or superstitious expectation of a wonder, or fanaticism, finding in it only faith and submission. Clarke goes the other way. The terror of the furnace will not move them, he says, and though they are equally determined if no rescue comes, they are satisfied that in some way God will deliver them out of the king's hand, since his power cannot reach them in the kingdom they would ascend to from his furnace.

Clarke draws the political rule out of it as well: render to the sovereign what is his, but where the sovereign claims what belongs to God his authority is to be resisted, God having no use for the sovereign's things and the sovereign no right to God's. On the second half of the sentence the readings converge again. Gill takes the men as resigned should God not think fit to exert a power they are well assured he has; Wesley says it was all one to them which way God chose to honour himself, they being resolved to suffer rather than sin, and puts the whole in a line — that God will deliver either from death or in death. Calvin makes their constancy rest on two supports, a settled persuasion that their lives were in God's keeping and would be given back if that were useful, and a readiness to die outright if he preferred that sacrifice; and he turns it on the reader, since most men fall away for want of confidence in the first, and scarcely one in a hundred holds it fixed in the heart, everyone taking his own way of preserving his life as though there were no strength in God at all.
19:
The king's fury is a study in temper. Henry expects the opposite, since a man who had owned so much of the true God might have been recalled by such an answer; passions indulged grow more violent and show in the face, and a prince who traded the majesty of the throne for the look of a wild bull in a net would have blushed to see himself in a glass. Clarke marvels at a man who had watched his authority overturned before and would try his strength again. Gill says simply that he was nettled to find his threats had made no impression.

The sevenfold heat is variously explained. Clarke takes seven for as hot as it could be made; Ellicott doubts it is a round number and offers a possibility worth weighing, that the Babylonians reckoned seven demons the most formidable of the infernal powers, so the figure may point to them, the punishment having a religious character and the overheating a religious act. He corrects the phrase to than it was fitting, and notes that the impropriety of the heating is what killed the executioners. Henry sees the cruelty in the direction of the change, since rank might have earned mitigation and got the opposite.

Who was ordered to do it is disputed. Gill takes the men for the most famous in the army for courage and strength, and Ellicott supposes they were chosen as likeliest to endure the heat, the army being evidently present. Clarke reads it the other way and makes them generals or chief officers, since mere strength was not what the task required. Wesley asks what the king can have been thinking — that three bound men would resist, or that their God would shield them, or that the strongest soldiers could prevail if he did — and answers that God meant to show his power when the king did his worst.

The clothing gets more attention than one expects, because of what happens to it. Clarke observes that one word occurs nowhere else in the older Scriptures, cites Herodotus for a Babylonian dress of linen and woollen tunics under a short white cloak, with a turban, and renders the list as cloaks, turbans, outer woollen tunics and under linen ones — the point being that the outermost garments are named, which is why the later verse about their being unaltered tells. Ellicott appeals to the same historian but orders them differently: the first an under-garment covering the whole body, the second a tunic spread over it, the third a cloak probably reserved for state occasions. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch keep to philology, the one allowing that an Arabic usage would make the first word breeches, the other denying they are hose and matching the word to a Semitic term for a tunic.

Then the executioners die, and everyone marks the contrast. Keil and Delitzsch explain the mechanics, that the furnace had a mouth above through which victims were thrown, a task ordinarily safe but not at this heat, and say the detail is recorded to measure the miracle. Ellicott sets the death of the men who carried out the sentence against the survival of those sentenced; Wesley makes the point sharper, that a flame which killed them outside could have killed the bound men more easily, before they landed. Calvin notes that at first sight God appears to desert his servants, no help showing itself, and that their courage never depended on expecting any; he distinguishes the two halves of the wonder, the outer edge of the fire consuming strong men by merely playing about them while those in its heart walked unharmed. Gill and Clarke both note that the old versions insert sixty-seven verses of a song absent from the Hebrew, Clarke adding that the join between this verse and the next is visibly broken.
24:
The king had been watching, Ellicott says, through an opening in the furnace wall. Gill takes his astonishment partly for the death of his own men and partly for a panic sent directly on him. Calvin reads the question put to the counsellors as arranged: the king could have gone to the furnace himself, but God meant the admission to come from the men who had engineered the affair, so the rescue could not be laid to any earthly cause.

What the king saw divides them sharply. Clarke calls the received rendering a most improper translation, asks what notion an idolatrous king could have of Christ, and insists the phrase means a son of the gods, a divine being or angel — precisely what the king calls the figure a few verses later. Wesley takes the older view, that the Angel of the covenant did sometimes appear before the incarnation, and draws from it that those who suffer for Christ have his presence with them in the furnace. Ellicott holds the middle. The words come from a heathen who calls the same person an angel four verses on, and the king probably imagined him standing to the God of Israel as he stood to his own god. The early fathers read it of Christ; beyond that we have no means of knowing, and must be content that the presence which went with Israel in the wilderness watched over them in Babylon.

Gill notices what the king reports: four men loose and walking separately, where three had gone in tied, and turns it to use, the furnace standing for affliction in which men are loosed from the hold of sin even while bound in every other sense.

The inspection is treated as evidence. Henry observes that the examination was made by princes who could not be suspected of partiality, which is what clears the miracle. Calvin rests the weight on the last item, that not even the smell of fire had passed on them, since fire consumes whatever is put to it; and he values the witnesses because they were the enemies. Clarke supplies the sceptical parallel and disposes of it: heathen priests were said to walk on hot coals unhurt, and a Latin poet describes it, but another writer explains that they oiled their feet first — whereas here the officers knew no such trick would answer.

On the confession the readings split. Clarke calls it a noble testimony from a heathen and asks what produced it: had the three been time-servers, the true God's name would never have been heard in Babylon. Henry takes it at its word, that God can extort acknowledgements of his blessedness from men ready to curse him. Gill and Calvin will not have it. Gill grants the force of conviction but denies a thorough conversion, since the king did not give up his own gods; Calvin presses hardest, holding that repentance consists not in one or two acts but in perseverance, that this man mingled his idols with the God he praised, and that the tell-tale is the pronoun, since he never calls that God his own.

The decree and promotion close it. Clarke notes that the edict does not require anyone to worship the God of Israel, only to speak of him with reverence; Calvin allows it is pious in itself while denying its author credit, since men carried by a blind impulse to vindicate God's glory deserve none. Keil and Delitzsch read the closing phrase as after this sort rather than this God, a visible deity suiting the heathen mind better than an invisible one. Clarke and Ellicott make the promotion a reinstatement. Calvin will not let that pass either: the whole province had seen these men thrown into a furnace and restored to office, so the story travelled as if three heralds had been sent through the country.
